title: Who tailors and where it is documented
blurb: Say who leads tailoring, in which activity, where the decisions are recorded and who approves them.
question: A project manager wants to use lighter highlight reports than the organization's standard method requires. In which activity is this decided, where is it recorded, and who approves it?

teach.h: Who tailors, and where it lives
teach.body: Formally, the project manager leads the 'agree the tailoring requirements' activity, the first activity of initiating a project. How PRINCE2, or the business's own standard method, will be applied and tailored must be documented and agreed. The decisions are recorded in the project initiation documentation (PID), which the project board approves when it authorizes the project. In plain English: the PM proposes the fit, the PID writes it down, the board signs it off.

head: Who
Part in tailoring
rows: Approves it in the PID at authorization
Sets standards the project must follow
teach.caption: The PM proposes and documents; the board decides. Deviations from the business's standard method are documented and agreed.

teach.body: The PID gives the direction and scope of the project and, with the current stage plan, acts as the 'contract' between the project manager and the board. It brings together the management products from initiation, including how the method is tailored. The version used to gain authorization is cross-checked, baselined and placed under change control, and the end project report later compares performance against it.

items.label: Board approves the PID when authorizing the project
Managing a stage boundary reviews and updates the PID

teach.caption: At stage boundaries the PID is reviewed and, if needed, updated: for example the management approaches, team structure or role descriptions.
A favourite exam near miss: tailoring the method versus defining the management approaches (benefits, change, commercial, communication, digital and data, issue, quality, risk, sustainability).

teach.h: Why it must be documented and agreed
teach.body: Tailoring changes how everyone on the project works: what reports look like, who holds which role, how formal the controls are. If those choices were not written down and agreed, the board could not hold the project manager to them and the team could not follow them. Recording them in the PID makes tailoring part of the agreed baseline for running the project.

At Kestrel Valley Trams, project manager Priya Nair starts initiation for a ticket-machine upgrade. Using 'agree the tailoring requirements', she adapts the company's standard method: two delivery stages, fortnightly highlight reports and the company's own term 'gateway' for a stage end. She records this in the PID. The board approves it when it authorizes the project. At the first stage boundary a new supplier joins, so role descriptions in the PID are updated.

teach.text: The project manager leads tailoring, but cannot sign it off alone: the board approves it as part of the PID when it authorizes the project. Tailoring decisions belong in the PID, not in the daily log, the lessons log or the project brief.

items: Activity: 'agree the tailoring requirements', the first activity of initiating a project.
The project manager leads it and documents the tailoring and any deviations.
Recorded in the project initiation documentation (PID).
Approved by the project board when it authorizes the project.
Reviewed and, if needed, updated at stage boundaries along with the rest of the PID.

summary: You can now say that the project manager leads 'agree the tailoring requirements' in initiating a project, that the decisions are documented in the PID, and that the board approves them when it authorizes the project. You also know the PID is reviewed and updated at stage boundaries.

A.q: Which role leads the 'agree the tailoring requirements' activity?
A.why: The project manager leads 'agree the tailoring requirements' in initiating a project (15.4.1).

whyNot.0: The executive, with the board, approves the tailoring through the PID; the PM leads the activity.
whyNot.2: Project assurance supports the board; it does not lead this activity.
whyNot.3: The senior supplier represents supplier interests on the board and does not lead tailoring.

A.q: In which process does the 'agree the tailoring requirements' activity take place?
A.why: 'Agree the tailoring requirements' is the first activity of initiating a project (15.4.1).

whyNot.0: Starting up a project prepares the project brief; tailoring is agreed in initiation.
whyNot.1: Directing a project is where the board approves the PID, but the activity itself is in initiation.
whyNot.2: Managing a stage boundary reviews and updates the PID later; it does not contain this activity.

A.q: Where are a project's tailoring decisions documented?
A.why: Tailoring decisions are recorded in the PID, which the board approves when it authorizes the project (2.7, 4.3.1).

whyNot.0: The outline business case justifies the project in starting up; it does not record tailoring.
whyNot.1: The project product description defines the final product and its quality expectations.
whyNot.3: The issue management approach sets how issues and changes are controlled, not how the whole method is tailored.

B.q: Who approves the tailoring of PRINCE2 for a project, and when?
options: The project board, when it authorizes the project
The project manager, when the PID is assembled
The business layer, when it issues the mandate
Project assurance, when the business case is ready
B.why: Tailoring is recorded in the PID, and the project board approves the PID when it authorizes the project (2.7).

whyNot.1: The PM leads and documents tailoring but does not approve it; the board does.
whyNot.2: The mandate comes before the project exists, long before tailoring is agreed.
whyNot.3: Project assurance advises the board; approval is a board decision.

B.q:
Which two statements about tailoring decisions are correct?
1. They are recorded in the PID.
2. Any deviation from the business's standard method is documented and agreed.
3. They are fixed once the project mandate is issued.
4. They are made in the 'agree the management approaches' activity.
B.why: Tailoring is recorded in the PID, and any deviation from the standard method must be documented and agreed (2.7, 15.4.1).

whyNot.1: Statement 4 is false: tailoring is agreed in 'agree the tailoring requirements', which comes before 'agree the management approaches'.
whyNot.2: Statement 3 is false: tailoring is agreed in initiation and can be revisited at stage boundaries.
whyNot.3: Both are false: tailoring is not set by the mandate, and it has its own activity.

B.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. In 'managing a stage boundary', the project manager reviews and, if necessary, updates the [?], including its management approaches and role descriptions.
B.why: An objective of managing a stage boundary is to review and if necessary update the PID, including approaches, team structure and role descriptions (18.2).

whyNot.0: The project brief is used in starting up and initiating; the PID replaces it as the baseline.
whyNot.1: The mandate comes from the business layer before the project starts and is not updated at stage boundaries.
whyNot.2: The lessons log records lessons; it does not hold the management approaches or role descriptions.

C.q: A project manager on a new council project wants simpler highlight reports than the council's standard method requires. What should happen?
options: PM records it in the daily log as an informal choice
Executive approves it in starting up, in the brief
Team managers agree it in checkpoint reports
PM agrees it in initiation; board approves the PID
C.why: The PM handles it in 'agree the tailoring requirements' during initiation, documents it in the PID, and the board approves the PID when authorizing the project (2.7, 15.4.1).

whyNot.0: Deviations from the standard method must be documented and agreed in the PID, not left as informal diary entries.
whyNot.1: Tailoring is agreed in initiating a project and recorded in the PID, not settled in the project brief.
whyNot.2: Checkpoint reports are team managers' progress reports to the PM; they do not agree project tailoring.

C.q: The PID has been authorized and baselined. At a stage boundary, the board wants a lighter reporting format for the next stage. Where and how is this handled?
options: In closing a project, by updating the lessons report
In managing a stage boundary, by updating the PID
In controlling a stage, by raising an exception report
In starting up a project, by updating the project brief
C.why: Managing a stage boundary reviews and, if necessary, updates the PID, so tailoring such as reporting format can be revisited there (18.2).

whyNot.0: Closing a project ends the project; it is not where the next stage's controls are set.
whyNot.2: Exception reports are for forecast breaches of stage tolerance, not for changing report formats.
whyNot.3: Starting up a project is long finished; the PID has replaced the brief as the baseline.

C.q: Which is the first activity of initiating a project, and who leads it?
options: Agree the management approaches; the project manager
Agree the tailoring requirements; the project executive
Agree the tailoring requirements; the project manager
Establish project controls; the project board
C.why: The first activity of initiating a project is 'agree the tailoring requirements', led by the project manager (15.4.1).

whyNot.0: 'Agree the management approaches' is the second activity; the approaches depend on the tailoring.
whyNot.1: The executive approves tailoring through the PID with the board; the PM leads the activity.
whyNot.3: 'Establish project controls' comes after the approaches are agreed, and the PM leads it.

reteach.title: The rulebook for this one project
reteach.question: Every project writes its own short rulebook for how PRINCE2 will be used. Who writes it, where is it kept, and who signs it?

blocks.body: The project manager writes it, in 'agree the tailoring requirements' at the start of initiation. It is kept in the PID, alongside the business case, plans and approaches. The project board signs it when it authorizes the project. At each stage boundary the PID is reviewed, so the rulebook can be updated if the project has changed.

blocks.text: Two activities sit side by side in initiation. 'Agree the tailoring requirements' decides how the method is applied; 'agree the management approaches' then sets the approaches for benefits, risk, quality and the rest.

explain.body: The project manager leads 'agree the tailoring requirements'. The PM may need to tailor PRINCE2, or the business's standard method, for internal and external factors. Any deviation is documented and agreed.

test.q: What must happen to any deviation from the business's standard project management method?
options: It must be reported in the next highlight report
It must be logged as an off-specification
It must be documented and agreed
It must be recorded in the lessons log
test.why: How the method is applied or tailored, including any deviation from the standard, must be documented and agreed (15.4.1).

whyNot.0: Highlight reports describe stage progress to the board; tailoring is agreed in initiation and recorded in the PID.
whyNot.1: An off-specification is a product that does not meet its specification, not a method deviation.
whyNot.3: The lessons log captures lessons; a deviation needs to be documented and agreed in the PID.

explain.body: The PID brings together the management products from initiation, including the tailoring. The authorized version is baselined and placed under change control.

test.q: Why does it matter that tailoring is recorded in the PID?
options: The PID is the PM's diary of actions and informal issues
The PID is sent to the business layer to set tolerances
The PID is the report that closes each management stage
The PID is the baseline the board authorizes and tracks
test.why: The authorized PID is baselined and later compared with actual performance, so tailoring recorded there becomes part of the agreed way of running the project (4.3.1).

whyNot.0: That describes the daily log, not the PID.
whyNot.1: The project board approves the PID when it authorizes the project; the PID is not sent to the business layer to set tolerances.
whyNot.2: Each stage is closed with an end stage report, not the PID.

explain.body: The project board approves the PID, and so the tailoring, when it authorizes the project in directing a project.

test.q: When does the project board approve the tailoring set out in the PID?
test.why: The board approves the PID, including tailoring, when it authorizes the project (2.7).

whyNot.0: When initiation is authorized, the PID does not yet exist; it is built during initiation.
whyNot.2: Closure comes at the end; the tailoring is needed from the start of delivery.
whyNot.3: Ongoing direction responds to requests and issues during a stage; it is not when the PID is approved.

explain.body: Managing a stage boundary reviews and, if necessary, updates the PID: management approaches, team structure and role descriptions. Tailoring can be adjusted there as the project changes.

test.q: Which process gives the chance to review and update tailoring as the project moves into a new stage?
test.why: Managing a stage boundary reviews and, if necessary, updates the PID, including its approaches and role descriptions (18.2).

whyNot.1: Managing product delivery is the team manager's process for delivering work packages.
whyNot.2: Controlling a stage manages day-to-day work within the stage, not changes to the PID baseline.
whyNot.3: Starting up a project happens before initiation, before any tailoring is agreed.
